# What goes here

How things are now, and why, as far as the code cannot tell it: why the code is so and what was rejected, with the
background, the cost and what would reverse it; how it should behave, where the code says only how it does; and what
lies outside the repository (the promises of a service it calls, the data in production, how to run or operate it).
A summary of how the code works does not go here: the code says that, and a copy goes stale. Open work goes in
issues, and what each task left behind in `docs/log.md`. Start from [index.md](index.md).

A document has two kinds of reader. Whoever changes the code reads what it does and why it was designed so, and the
document follows that code. Whoever runs it, or meets a failure, reads the procedures, the alarms and the costs
measured, and the document follows the scripts and the configuration they rely on.

A shape that code can generate exactly (an OpenAPI document, a schema) stays generated. The knowledge document links
to it and says what the code cannot: why it has this shape, and what changing it promises.

# One document

One document is one file, `docs/knowledge/<slug>.md`. The slug never changes once the file exists, because commit
messages and other documents refer to it. The frontmatter holds no YAML comment, which is read as nothing: quote a
value with a `#` after a space in it (`title: 'PR #1 is merged'`).

| Field | Content |
|---|---|
| `type` | `Knowledge` |
| `title` | Display name |
| `description` | One sentence: what the document tells |
| `tags` | Exactly one area, one of the `areas` declared in `.config/rotproof.toml`. The index groups documents by it, in that order |
| `status` | `stable` (holds) or `deprecated` (no longer holds) |
| `match` | Only for an alarm, and optional: a list of short strings, each as it appears in what is observed. See "Alarms" |
| `verified` | Optional: who reviewed the document and on which day, `{by: human:<name>, at: YYYY-MM-DD}`, read from the clock |
| `stale_after` | Optional: the day to look at it again, for what it says of outside the code, which `follows` cannot watch (a service's promise, data in production). From that day `rotproof check` warns of it on every run and fails nothing: measure again, then write the day in `verified` and the next one here |

The body is free, except that a deprecated document opens with `# Resolution`: what replaced it, and that an alarm has
`# When` and `# Do`.

# Rules

- **Edit in place.** When things change, change the document in the same piece of work. It describes the present;
  git keeps its history.
- **A document that no longer holds stays.** Set `status: deprecated` and write `# Resolution` as the first heading:
  what replaced it. Deleting it breaks the links to it.
- **A document that describes code follows it.** It names what it describes in `follows`, each with its hash when
  the document was last reviewed against it, and `rotproof check` fails when one of them changed since, naming the
  command that pins it once the document is reviewed:

  ```yaml
  follows:
    src/api/routes.py: "3e1f0a9c"
    src/api/routes.py::create_user: "0b7d21e4"
    src/api/routes.py::Router.add: "9a01c3ff"
    src/api/: "51c0d2aa"
  ```

  A key is a file, in any language (`src/api/routes.py`); a definition in a Python, TypeScript, JavaScript or Rust file,
  written `<file>::<Name>.<Name>` in all of them (`::create_user`, a method `::Router.add`, `cli.rs::Command.Before`);
  or a directory, for every file under it that Rotproof reads as code (`.py`, `.rs`, `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.js` and the other
  TypeScript and JavaScript extensions), whatever the stack (`src/api/`). Every definition counts, exported or not: in
  Python a function or class and its methods; in TypeScript and JavaScript a function, class, interface, type, enum,
  namespace or variable (`export const f = () => ...`), the members of a class, interface and enum, and `default` for
  an `export default` with no name; in Rust a `fn`, `struct`, `enum` and its variants, `union`, `trait` and its items,
  `type`, `const`, `static`, `macro_rules!` and an inline `mod` with its items (`tests.helper`). A Rust type's key
  covers its definition and every `impl` block for it in the file, and `Type.method` the method of that name in any of
  them. What a macro defines is not seen.

  `rotproof follows knowledge/api.md <key>...` writes these lines, with the hashes as the code is now: run it when a
  document starts to follow something, once the document says what the code does, and when the check names it. It pins
  only the keys named, all of them or none, and a key not in `follows` is added at its end. A hash is quoted, as YAML
  reads `12345678` as a number.
  A definition is hashed from its first decorator or attribute to its end (a Rust `///` doc comment is an attribute),
  so a change elsewhere in its file does not fail it. A name that is more than one piece in its file (overloads, a
  getter and its setter, a Python `@property` and its `@x.setter`, the `impl` blocks of a type) is hashed on all of
  them, in the order they appear. What a document follows must exist: a file, directory or definition that is gone
  fails. Writing the new hash changes the document, so its commit records the review. A document about a decision
  follows nothing. After a refactoring that kept what the code does, a person re-pins every changed hash in one act
  with `rotproof approve --reviewed`, on a terminal.

# Alarms

Some knowledge matters only when something is seen: a service starts refusing requests, a CI image moves, a build
prints a warning it never printed. "When X is seen, do Y" holds as long as the system is as it is, so it is knowledge,
not work: there is no work waiting yet, and no moment that is sure to come. A document with these two headings is an
alarm:

| Heading | Content |
|---|---|
| `# When` | What is seen, and where: the strings as they were observed (an error message, an exit code, an HTTP status), not in other words, and the job or the command whose output shows them |
| `# Do` | What to do then. Usually: open an issue for the work, and what to look at first |

- **Write what is seen as it is seen.** Whoever meets the message searches `docs/` for it before anything else, and
  finds the alarm only if its words are the message's words. When a version of a tool changes the wording, write each
  wording, and set `stale_after` to the day to look again: `rotproof check` warns of it from then.
- **`match` holds the parts that stay.** Short strings that appear in the output as they are (`403`,
  `trusted publisher`), so a search finds the alarm even when the rest of the message changed. `tags` holds the area,
  so the strings have a field of their own. A number is matched as the text it is printed as.
- **An alarm is not an issue.** A moment that may never come would keep an issue open forever, though no work waits
  yet.
- **Noticing the symptom is not something the records can guarantee.** Rotproof does not search by meaning: an answer
  that changes from one asking to the next is not a check. Searching for the exact string is.

`rotproof check` fails when an alarm has one of `# When` and `# Do` without the other, or when either is empty, and
when a document that is no alarm has `match`. Whether `# When` is in the observed words, and not in other words, it
cannot see: that is for the writer.

# Index

[index.md](index.md) is generated: the documents left out under `# Left out`, each with why, as an alarm left out is
not shown until it is fixed; the alarms under `# When something happens`, each with the first sentence of what
is seen and its `match` strings, as reading the index before work is what watches for them; then the other documents
by area; then the deprecated ones under `# Closed`. After adding or changing a document, run `rotproof index`.
`rotproof check` fails when the index differs from what `rotproof index` writes.
